what_it_does: Finding the best strategy for an agent making decisions in an uncertain environment (a Markov Decision Process, or MDP) normally requires evaluating every possible action at every state in every iteration — a process that gets extremely slow as the number of actions grows. SwiftVI speeds this up by using a priority queue (a data structure that always surfaces the most promising item first) to avoid evaluating actions that provably cannot be the best choice, cutting runtime substantially without changing the answer.
method_in_detail:
The idea. The standard algorithm for solving these decision problems — called value iteration (VI) — repeatedly estimates how good each state is by looking at every action available from that state and picking the best one. If a state has 100 actions, all 100 get evaluated every iteration even though only one will win. SwiftVI exploits a key mathematical property: if the estimates are initialized from above the true answer and updated carefully, those estimates can only decrease over time (they are monotonically non-increasing). This means an action's score this iteration is always at least as good as its score in any future iteration.

How it works. SwiftVI maintains a max-heap — think of it as a sorted list where the highest-scoring item is always on top — of upper-bound scores for every action at each state. To update a state, the algorithm pulls the top action (highest score) from the heap, recomputes its score using the current estimates of neighboring states, and pushes the updated score back in. If after this update the same action is still on top, its score is the answer for this state in this iteration — no other actions need to be evaluated at all. If a different action takes the top spot, the process repeats until the winner stabilizes, which often takes just 1–3 recomputations even when hundreds of actions exist.

The key design choice. Because upper-bound scores can only go down over time, any action whose highest possible future score already falls below the current best lower bound can be permanently removed from the heap and ignored forever. This permanent pruning (action elimination) means later iterations get progressively cheaper as the heap shrinks.

The result. SwiftVI comes in four variants (VIH, VIAE, VIAEH, VIAEHL) that combine heaps and action elimination in different ways. On random MDPs and real-world cloud management and maze-navigation problems, the top variants — particularly VIH and VIAEHL — outperform standard value iteration and the previous best algorithm (BAO) across a range of state and action sizes, with advantages growing as the number of actions increases. When plugged into reinforcement-learning algorithms that use value iteration as a subroutine, SwiftVI cuts their total runtime substantially at tight accuracy targets.
